summary: The registration policy for the NETCONF Capability URNs registry, set by RFC 6241, was stricter than needed. This best current practice changes it to IETF Review, which also allows registrations from certain well-reviewed Experimental RFCs. It updates RFC 6241.

eli5.summary: The club's membership rule was too strict. This makes it a little easier for reviewed ideas to get on the official list.

subtitle: Relaxes the registration policy for NETCONF capability identifiers.

tldr.problem: RFC 6241 set the NETCONF Capability URNs registry to Standards Action policy, allowing only Standards Track RFCs to register, which proved too restrictive.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7803 changes the policy to IETF Review, allowing well-reviewed Experimental RFCs and other non-Standards-Track documents to register NETCONF capabilities.
tldr.outcome: Registry access is more flexible while maintaining careful review, reducing the need for IESG exceptions.

today: RFC 7803 is a Best Current Practice and updates RFC 6241. The NETCONF Capability URNs registry now accepts entries from well-reviewed Experimental and other non-Standards-Track RFCs.

sections.title: Relaxing Registry Access
sections.content: RFC 6241 defined NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol) and set up an IANA registry for NETCONF Capability URNs. The registry originally used the 'Standards Action' policy, which means only Standards Track RFCs could register entries. This policy was intended to ensure thorough review. However, it became clear that useful Experimental RFCs and other well-reviewed work needed capability URN allocations, and the strict policy required IESG exceptions to allow them.
sections.eli5: A registry for network configuration standards was closed except to official standards. It turned out to be too strict.

sections.title: The New IETF Review Policy
sections.content: RFC 7803 changes the policy to 'IETF Review'. This allows registrations from Standards Track RFCs as before, but also from well-reviewed Experimental RFCs, Informational RFCs (for example, to correct registry errors), and other RFCs, provided they go through IETF Last Call and consultation with relevant working groups. The Operations and Management Area Directors confirm that the document received appropriate review during IESG evaluation.
sections.eli5: Now the registry accepts names from official standards, but also from experimental work that has been carefully reviewed and approved by the IETF community.

sections.title: Implementation and Impact
sections.content: This policy change has had real impact on the NETCONF ecosystem. By allowing Experimental RFCs to register capabilities when carefully reviewed, the working group can now document and register extensions sooner. The Operations and Management Area Directors verify that non-Standards-Track RFCs receive appropriate review. This balance maintains quality while reducing procedural barriers.
sections.eli5: The new rule makes it easier for new ideas to get official names, as long as they are carefully checked.

references.text: Enns, R., Ed., Bjorklund, M., Ed., Schoenwaelder, J., Ed., and A. Bierman, Ed., "Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF)", RFC 6241, June 2011.
Narten, T. and H. Alvestrand, "Guidelines for Writing an IANA Considerations Section in RFCs", BCP 26, RFC 5226, May 2008.
